name: Reporting Under More Than One Standard
title: Reporting Under More Than One Standard
answer: Reporting under more than one standard means preparing financial statements and disclosures that satisfy two or more accounting frameworks, such as local GAAP and IFRS, or US GAAP and IFRS. It covers the primary statements, notes, segment data, and the reconciliations that explain why numbers differ between frameworks. The work sits in financial reporting and synthesis, where the same underlying transactions must be tagged, translated, and presented under each standard's recognition, measurement, and disclosure rules. It also includes the audit trail that shows how each reported figure was derived.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Reporting under more than one standard means preparing financial statements and disclosures that satisfy two or more accounting frameworks, such as local GAAP and IFRS, or US GAAP and IFRS. It covers the primary statements, notes, segment data, and the reconciliations that explain why numbers differ between frameworks. The work sits in financial reporting and synthesis, where the same underlying transactions must be tagged, translated, and presented under each standard's recognition, measurement, and disclosure rules. It also includes the audit trail that shows how each reported figure was derived.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on the general ledger and ERP systems that hold the source transactions, plus consolidation and reporting platforms that store multiple charts of accounts and standard-specific mappings. Data warehouses, ETL pipelines, and APIs move balances and metadata into a reporting layer, often with XBRL taxonomies for structured filing. Spreadsheets remain common for last-mile adjustments, reconciliations, and disclosure support. AI tools may sit alongside these systems to classify accounts, suggest mappings, or extract text from contracts and notes.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The method starts with a common trial balance and a mapping table that links each account to the relevant line item under each standard. Difference engines then apply recognition and measurement rules, such as lease accounting or revenue recognition, to produce standard-specific adjustments. Reconciliation reports compare the two outputs and flag unexplained variances for review. Natural language processing can help draft and check disclosure text, while rules and machine learning models can propose journal entries or classify transactions. A human reviewer confirms the adjustments and signs off on the final statements.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Governance covers controls over the mapping tables, adjustment rules, and model outputs, with version history and data lineage for every reported number. Because the same transaction may be measured differently under each standard, the audit trail must show the source data, the standard applied, and the reviewer who approved the change. Access controls and segregation of duties keep preparers, reviewers, and system administrators separate. Where AI is used, model risk management, explainability, and validation against known outcomes are part of the control environment. Disclosure and filing requirements shape much of this work, so the control framework must be documented and testable.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward more automated multi-standard reporting, with mapping and reconciliation increasingly handled by rules engines and AI assistants. Standard setters continue to work on convergence and interoperability, but differences in recognition, measurement, and disclosure are likely to remain. Structured data formats and digital filing will make it easier to compare outputs across frameworks. Finance teams will spend less time on manual mapping and more on reviewing exceptions, explaining variances, and improving the quality of the underlying data. The vocabulary and tooling around this work will keep expanding as more jurisdictions adopt or revise their reporting requirements.
